item.content:encoded:
Okay, I've finally worked up the courage to post this, let's see how it plays out. Writing an -EX has been a goal of mine since I started contributing to the site, and this is the closest I could get — it may not be technically explained, but it's still valid in-universe. I also wanted to write something that was literally just a monster, and a large, carnivorous, nocturnal mammal fit the bill nicely.

The whole thing was inspired by me walking my dog on a field at night, and realising I could only see her through the corner of my eye — this article explains the phenomenon pretty well. In any case, I hope you enjoy my scip about an invisible creature that may or may not exist.

Okay, this is going to be a weird one to explain — ironic, now I think about it — so bear with me while I try to deconstruct this for y'all.

Basically, what I wanted to achieve with the article was this: I wanted it to be layered. There are multiple possible ways of interpreting what's going on here, but the real symbolic 'meat' of the article comes (for me at least) when you start pulling it apart. I took an SCP about writing a fictional SCP, and intentionally made it slightly unclear whether it was actually fictional — for us (the readers), that's suspension of disbelief: the thing that makes horror scary, and the scp wiki interesting. You don't know whether this thing was real and became fictional, was real and made people think it became fictional, or was never real and was always fictional — that same 'unknowing' is parodied within the article itself through the slow loss of information and inability to comprehend it. The iterative process is intentionally similar to the way our own articles are constructed, starting from a base concept and developing, and I'm proud of the way that, at the end, the researchers dismiss the threat — after all, as scary as the SCP (wiki) might be, there's no way it could possibly be real.

Everything from the title to the core idea is designed to mimic and parody the reading and writing of SCP articles, both in-universe and out, and I honestly don't care whether it came through at all — it's the most 'artsy' thing I've ever attempted, and I'm proud of the result.

To conclude, I want to stress that there isn't any canonical answer to which interpretation is correct: there are three layers of meta going on here, and picking them apart to find an answer is downright impossible. There simply isn't enough information there. I have a headcanon for which is the 'real' one, if that term can be applied to a fictional narrative about a (maybe) fictional document about a (maybe) fictional creature, but that doesn't make yours any less correct. After all, it's just a story.
